> We must accept our reality in all its immensity. Everything, even the
> unheard of, must be possible within it. … This is, in the end, the only
> courage required of us: the courage to meet what is strangest and most
> awesome.
>
> — Rainer Maria Rilke, translated by Joanna Macy and Anita Barrows

## Source

The words are Rilke's, from *Letters to a Young Poet*: ten letters he wrote
between 1903 and 1908 to Franz Kappus, a young military cadet who wanted to be
a poet. This one is the eighth letter, written from Sweden in August 1904.

The wording above is from Macy and Barrows's *Letters to a Young Poet: A New
Translation and Commentary* (2021). Macy read the passage aloud in an
[On Being interview](https://onbeing.org/?p=1373595) with Barrows. Older
translations have Rilke asking for courage before what is "strangest, most
singular and most inexplicable"; "awesome" is the new translators' choice.

## Live the Questions

The same book holds Rilke's better-known advice to live the questions, from
the fourth letter, written at Worpswede on 16 July 1903:

> I want to ask you, as clearly as I can, to bear with patience all that is
> unresolved in your heart, and try to love the questions themselves, as if
> they were rooms yet to enter or books written in a foreign language. Don't
> dig for answers that can't be given you yet: you cannot live them now. For
> everything must be lived. Live the questions now, perhaps then, someday, you
> will gradually, without noticing, live into the answer.

The translation is as given on
[The Floating Library](https://thefloatinglibrary.com/2010/02/18/live-the-questions/),
which does not name the translator.

The two passages ask the same thing of Kappus a year apart: stay with what is
not yet understood, without forcing an answer and without retreating to the
familiar. Living the questions is the patience; meeting what is strangest is
the courage that patience takes.
